Recent research separates semantic resemblance from factual support. A 2025–2026 recommendation study found high BERTScore similarity despite low statement-level factual precision; its review-based evidence is unavailable here, but the distinction remains useful ([study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24366)). ACL 2024 also finds explanation faithfulness depends on model, task and explanation type, motivating perturbation checks rather than trusting plausible rationales ([paper](https://aclanthology.org/2024.findings-acl.19/)).

Suggested audit adaptation: attach exact title/description spans, item IDs and history timestamps to each claim; label compatibility as supported, explicitly contradicted or unknown. Missing specifications mean unknown, not incompatibility. Interaction history establishes observed interaction, not ownership or immediate need. Compare direct recent-interest matches against broad semantic matches using a predefined rubric; treat their preferred ordering as a hypothesis to validate, not an established universal rule. These checks can use deterministic text matching and manual review without pretrained downloads.

Abstain from unsupported compatibility, ownership and immediate-usefulness claims while retaining the required recommendation rankings. A 2026 catalog-faithfulness audit found verbalized confidence poorly distinguished valid recommendations from hallucinations and showed that matcher choice substantially changed measured error; it validated its measurement against human judgments ([paper, corrected version](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10008v3)). For this task, manually review a small sample across all four categories, including explicit conflicts, missing descriptions and direct-versus-broad matches. Report evidence-supported claim precision, contradiction-detection precision/recall, abstention coverage and reviewer agreement separately from the fixed macro validation HR@10. This is a proposed audit protocol, not a validated result.
